name: Quaker Blue
lede: Quaker Blue is a near-black, slate-dark blue that Maerz and Paul recorded in 1892, an adjective likely borrowed from the plain, dark clothing associated with Quakers.

sections.title: A plain color, by name
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color dates the name to 1892 and places it at plate 40 E 6 [1]. The dictionary does not spell out the reasoning, but *Quaker* was a common Victorian shorthand for a drab, undyed grey or near-black, the sober dress Quakers were known for [1]. Maerz and Paul paired it with a very different color under the same word, the warm grey [[pebble-grey|Quaker Drab]], suggesting the adjective described a plainness of dress rather than one fixed hue [1].

The nearest ISCC-NBS block by computed distance is 187, black, but the match is loose, 5.2 units off, so the 1955 dictionary never quite caught this exact mix [1]. In Lab terms it sits close to [[graphite|Graphite]] and [[gunmetal|Gunmetal]], both under five units away, and to [[black-grey|Black Grey]] a little further out [1]. No Munsell notation is recorded for it, unlike most of its library neighbors [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of it covers at least 5 percent of the canvas in 627 of our 23,781 archive paintings, as photographed, more common than 78 percent of our named colors [2]. It most often serves as a shadow tone, 39 percent of the 346 paintings where our within-painting lens finds it [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1200s, at 2.9 times the rate expected from that century's baseline [2]. The earliest dated painting carrying it is from 1099, 831 years before Maerz and Paul's 1892 record, a floor set by the archive's thin early coverage rather than a true first appearance [2]. John Singer Sargent carries it in 8 of his 287 works here [2].
